specAnchors.text: understand how the use of fertiliser can increase crop yield

primer.text: Fertiliser is the quiet engine of modern crop yields. This note explains why repeated harvesting strips mineral ions from farmland, how replacing them lets crops grow larger and faster, and which ions matter most — magnesium for chlorophyll, nitrate for amino acids — plus the deficiency signs that reveal them.

modules.title: Feeding the Soil to Feed the Crop
modules.opening: Every harvest carries mineral ions off the field inside the crop itself, so growing the same crop year after year drains the soil. Fertilisers replace those ions, letting crop plants grow faster and bigger, which lifts the yield the farmer collects.
keyPoints: Plants need a range of mineral ions from the soil to grow well.
Repeated cropping drains those ions, so they must be replaced between seasons.
Fertilisers supply the missing ions and push crops to grow faster and larger, raising yields.
Organic options include farmyard manure and compost, while chemical fertilisers arrive as dry granules or liquid sprays.

low.restatement: Crops eat the soil's minerals; fertiliser puts them back so the next crop grows bigger.
low.analogy: A repeated bank withdrawal finally needs a deposit — fertiliser is the farmer's top-up.
low.examPointer: Tie the yield gain to the growth gain: bigger, faster plants simply harvest more mass per field.

medium.restatement: Crop plants absorb mineral ions continuously, and each harvest removes them from the field; applying fertiliser, whether organic manure or chemical granules and sprays, replenishes the supply so the next crop grows faster and larger and the yield rises.
medium.analogy: Refilling the pantry after every meal cooked, so the next batch never runs short of ingredients.
medium.examPointer: Name both fertiliser families — organic and chemical — when asked how ions are replaced.

modules.title: Mineral Ions and Their Deficiency Clues
sourceHeadings: Using fertilisers to increase crop yields
modules.opening: Each mineral ion does a specific building job inside a plant, and each shortage writes its own symptom on the leaves. Magnesium builds chlorophyll, nitrate builds amino acids for proteins, and the exam expects both pairs learned precisely.
keyPoints: Magnesium ions are needed to build chlorophyll, and a shortage shows as yellowing leaves.
Nitrate ions are needed to build amino acids, the blocks of proteins, and shortage brings weak growth with yellowing leaves.
Phosphate supports storage and transfer chemistry, calcium strengthens walls and membranes, and potassium assists stomatal opening.
Spelling matters in the exam: crops need nitrate ions, never nitrites or nitrogen gas.

low.restatement: Magnesium makes the green stuff, nitrate makes proteins; short-change the plant and the leaves go yellow.
low.analogy: A builder short of one material — no bricks, no wall; the visible crack tells you which lorry never arrived.
low.examPointer: Learn the two required pairs as locked couples: magnesium with chlorophyll, nitrate with amino acids.

medium.restatement: Magnesium ions form part of chlorophyll, so deficient plants show yellowing leaves; nitrate ions supply the nitrogen for amino acids and therefore proteins, so deficient plants grow weakly with yellowing foliage; phosphate, calcium and potassium each underpin their own structures with distinct deficiency signs.
medium.analogy: Each ion is a key for a different workshop inside the leaf — lose one key and that workshop's output stops.
medium.examPointer: Write nitrate with care in the exam; nitrite or nitrogen loses the mark instantly.

glossary.definition: A material added to soil to replace or boost the mineral ions available to crop plants.
The mass of crop harvested from a given area of land.
Dissolved inorganic ions such as nitrate and magnesium that plants absorb from soil.
The green pigment that captures light energy for photosynthesis.
